title: Audrey Werro through to European Championships 800m final after fall
content:
Audrey Werro, the fastest woman this year over 800m, has been handed a lifeline at the European Championships after falling in the semi-finals.

The 22-year-old rising Swiss athlete was leading the race at 650m when, around the final bend, she tripped and fell. She got up and finished the semi final in last (eighth) place, with a time of 2:35.35s.

Video footage from the reverse angle of the fall shows that Werro’s right foot connected with the left arm of French athlete Anais Bourgoin. That caused Werro’s right foot to turn inwards and then she clipped her left calf, stumbling onto the rail as she hit the track.

Great Britain’s Jemma Reekie won the race (1:58.61s) at the Alexander Stadium in Birmingham, England, navigating the chaos to move up the field from fourth at 600m. Bourgoin finished second and third-place Veronica Vancardo, the other Swiss athlete, also advanced to Friday’s final.

“I don’t know, I can’t explain what happened,” a slightly dazed Werro told reporters, speaking in French, in the mixed zone. “I have to see what happened in the video. While I was running, I felt good, and a second after, I was on the floor. It seemed like there was a lot of movement at the back, maybe my foot was touched.”

A floored Werro inadvertently took out Gabija Galvydyte of Lithuania, who also got up to finish in 2:03.59s, with the rules clear that athletes must finish in order to appeal.

European Athletics later confirmed following a review from the referee that Werro would advance to Friday’s final, citing “Technical Rule 17.1.1” in relation to “unintentional touch”. Galvydyte also advanced, though much sooner than Werro. “We’re going to see what we can do, if it’s possible to discuss (with officials), to make the final,” she said in the mixed zone, shortly before being reinstated.

This is partly the nature of championship racing, with eight women contesting for three spots and immense depth in the 800m.

Werro led the field at halfway, running a balanced 58.8s for the opening 400m. The six athletes to stay on their feet all broke two minutes, with all eight women in the second semi-final — won by GB’s Keely Hodgkinson in 1:57.38s — under that barrier too.

“It was a deliberate choice to control the race and manage the pace,” Werro told reporters of her positioning at the front of the pack, and slowing from 400m to 600m. “I think running at the front is always safer, but today it was a little risky.”

There seems to be no lasting damage. “I’m okay, just some scratches,” she said, sporting black marks across her red Switzerland vest. Her bib was ripped off when she fell.

Last summer Werro won the Diamond League final and in March took silver at the World Indoor Championships behind Hodgkinson. Her rise has been rapid and her time-trialling credentials are unmatched in the modern era — she became the third-fastest woman of all-time over 800m when she ran 1:53.80s to beat Hodgkinson at the Stockholm Diamond League this June, the quickest performance since the world record by Jarmila Kratochvilova in 1983.

As a championship racer, she is still learning. Up until last year, Werro was competing internationally at age-group level. Hodgkinson, who holds Olympic, world indoor and European titles, showed her smarts by winding up the pace inside the last 200m, whereas Werro allowed the field to condense around her.

It sets up a blockbuster final. Hodgkinson, who set an 800m indoor world record in February (beating Werro in the process) is chasing her fifth European crown and third continental outdoor title.

Also in the medal hunt is Femke Broeders-Bol, who boasts Olympic medals and two world titles in the 400m hurdles. This her first season as a two-lap runner. She finished less than one-tenth behind Hodgkinson in the second semi-final.

The final on Friday will feature 10 women instead of the usual eight: the top three from each heat, the advanced Werro and Galvydyte, plus the two fastest non-automatic qualifiers — Switzerland’s Valentina Rosamilia and Frenchwoman Clara Lieberman, who both ran PBs of 1:58.

Five women have broken 1:56 this year, and four of them are here in Birmingham: Broeders-Bol, Werro, Hodgkinson and Bourgoin. It promises to be one of the great two-lap races, with Olga Mineyeva’s championship record of 1:55.41s very much at risk.
